results.title: Nonterminals in outputs have no empty production
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar in Chomsky normal form. If a nonterminal $B$ occurs in the output of some production of $g$, then $g$ has no production $B \to \varepsilon$.

results.title: Forms yielding the empty word under Chomsky normal form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $g$ is in Chomsky normal form, then every symbol of a sentential form that yields the empty word is a nonterminal $B$ for which $g$ has a production $B \to \varepsilon$.

results.title: Shape of yields under Chomsky normal form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar in Chomsky normal form, $A$ a nonterminal and $w$ a nonempty word. Then $A$ yields $w$ if and only if $g$ has a production $A \to a$ with $a$ a terminal and $w = a$, or a production $A \to BC$ with nonterminals $B$ and $C$ and nonempty words $w_1$ and $w_2$ such that $w = w_1 w_2$, $B$ yields $w_1$ and $C$ yields $w_2$.

results.title: The CYK cell built from given cells
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given an assignment $f$ of a cell (a finite set of nonterminals of $g$) to every word, the cell of a word $w$ built from $f$ is the set of left-hand sides of those productions of $g$ whose outputs fit $w$ with respect to $f$.

results.title: The unshared CYK recurrence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The depth-$n$ CYK cell of a word $w$ is defined by recursion on $n$: at depth $0$ every cell is empty, and the depth-$(n + 1)$ cell of $w$ is the CYK cell of $w$ built from the depth-$n$ cells of all words. Cells are recomputed without sharing.

results.title: Correctness of the CYK recurrence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar in Chomsky normal form. For every natural number $n$, every nonterminal $A$ and every nonempty word $w$ of length at most $n$, $A$ lies in the depth-$n$ CYK cell of $w$ if and only if $A$ yields $w$.

results.title: Looking up a word in a CYK table
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a table listing pairs of a word and a cell, the cell recorded for a word $u$ is the cell of the first entry whose word is $u$, or the empty set if no entry has word $u$.

results.title: The CYK table
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The CYK table of a word $w$ up to length $l$ is a list of pairs of a word and a cell, defined by recursion on $l$. Up to length $0$ it is empty. The table up to length $l + 1$ is the table $t$ up to length $l$ followed by one entry for each position $i$ (counted from $0$) with $i + l + 1 \le |w|$, in increasing order of $i$: the factor $u$ of $w$ of length $l + 1$ starting at position $i$, together with the CYK…

results.title: Correct CYK tables
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A table listing pairs $(u, X)$ of a word $u$ and a set $X$ of nonterminals of $g$ is correct when, for every entry $(u, X)$ with $u$ nonempty, $X$ consists exactly of the nonterminals $B$ such that the one-symbol form $B$ yields $u$.

results.title: Correctness of the CYK table
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar in Chomsky normal form and $w$ a word. For every $l$, the CYK table of $w$ up to length $l$ is correct, and for all $j$ and $m$ with $0 < m \le l$ and $j + m \le |w|$, some entry of the table has as its word the factor of $w$ of length $m$ starting at position $j$ (positions counted from $0$).

results.title: The CYK recognizer
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar with initial nonterminal $S$. The CYK recognizer accepts the empty word exactly when $g$ has a production $S \to \varepsilon$, and accepts a nonempty word $w$ exactly when $S$ lies in the cell recorded for $w$ in the CYK table of $w$ up to length $|w|$.

results.title: Correctness of the CYK recognizer
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $g$ be a context-free grammar in Chomsky normal form. For every word $w$ over the terminals of $g$, the CYK recognizer accepts $w$ if and only if $w$ belongs to the language of $g$.

results.title: Players of a parity game
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A parity game has exactly two players, the even player and the odd player.

results.title: Opponent
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The opponent of a player of a parity game is the other player: the opponent of the even player is the odd player, and the opponent of the odd player is the even player.

results.title: Every player is $p$ or the opponent of $p$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all players $p$ and $q$ of a parity game, $q = p$ or $q$ is the opponent of $p$.

reading_title.source: Every player is $p$ or the opponent of $p$

results.title: Parity winning condition of a player
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A player wins an infinite sequence of natural-number priorities when the sequence satisfies that player's parity condition: the even player wins it when the largest priority occurring infinitely often exists and is even, and the odd player wins it when the largest priority occurring infinitely often exists and is odd.

results.title: Parity game
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A parity game on a type of positions consists of an owner for each position, which is one of the two players, a move relation between positions, where the owner of $v$ may move from $v$ to $w$ when $v$ is related to $w$, and a natural-number priority for each position, such that every position has at least one move (there are no dead ends).

results.title: Plays of a parity game
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An infinite sequence of positions $\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots$ of a parity game is a play if for every $i$ there is a move from $\pi_i$ to $\pi_{i+1}$.

results.title: Winner of a play in a parity game
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, write $\Omega(v)$ for the priority of a position $v$, and let $p$ be a player. An infinite sequence $\pi = \pi_0 \pi_1 \pi_2 \dots$ of positions of $G$ is won by $p$ when its priority sequence $\Omega(\pi_0) \Omega(\pi_1) \Omega(\pi_2) \dots$ satisfies the parity condition of $p$: among the priorities occurring infinitely often there is a largest one, and it is even if $p$ is the even…

results.title: Positional strategy in a parity game
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A positional (memoryless) strategy for player `p`: a choice of successor at each position, legal at the positions `p` owns. Its values elsewhere are irrelevant.

results.title: Positional strategies exist
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a parity game, every player has a positional strategy, since every position has a move.

results.title: Plays conforming to a strategy
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a positional strategy of player $p$ in a parity game. An infinite sequence of positions $\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots$ (not necessarily a play) conforms to $\sigma$ if $\pi_{i+1} = \sigma(\pi_i)$ for every $i$ such that $p$ owns $\pi_i$.

results.title: Winning strategy from a position
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p$ be a player of a parity game. A positional strategy $\sigma$ of $p$ wins from a position $v$ when every play starting at $v$ that conforms to $\sigma$ (at every position owned by $p$, the play moves to the successor chosen by $\sigma$) is won by $p$.

results.title: Winning region of a parity game
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The positions from which player `p` has a winning positional strategy.

results.title: Bounded priorities give every play a winner
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a player of a parity game in which every position has priority at most $d$, for some natural number $d$. Then every infinite sequence of positions, in particular every play, is won by $p$ or by the opponent of $p$.

results.title: No play is won by both players
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a parity game, for every player $p$, no infinite sequence of positions (play or not) is won both by $p$ and by the opponent of $p$.

results.title: Winning is prefix independent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a player of a parity game, $\pi = (\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots)$ an infinite sequence of positions and $j$ a natural number. Then the sequence $(\pi_j, \pi_{j+1}, \dots)$, obtained by dropping the first $j$ positions of $\pi$, is won by $p$ if and only if $\pi$ is won by $p$.

results.title: Joint successor of two strategies
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a positional strategy of player $p$ and $\tau$ a positional strategy of the opponent of $p$ in a parity game. The joint successor of a position $v$ is $\sigma(v)$ if $p$ owns $v$, and $\tau(v)$ otherwise.

results.title: Outcome of two positional strategies
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p$ be a player of a parity game, $\sigma$ a positional strategy of $p$ and $\tau$ a positional strategy of the opponent of $p$. The outcome of $\sigma$ and $\tau$ from a position $v$ is the infinite sequence of positions $v_0, v_1, v_2, \dots$ with $v_0 = v$ in which $v_{i+1}$ is the successor chosen by $\sigma$ at $v_i$ if $p$ owns $v_i$, and the successor chosen by $\tau$ at $v_i$ otherwise. It is the play…

results.title: The winning regions of the two players are disjoint
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a parity game, for every player $p$, no position lies both in the winning region of $p$ and in the winning region of the opponent of $p$.

results.title: Winning strategies keep winning along allowed moves
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a parity game, let $\sigma$ be a positional strategy of player $p$ that wins from a position $v$, and let $w$ be a position with a move from $v$ to $w$ such that $w = \sigma(v)$ if $p$ owns $v$. Then $\sigma$ wins from $w$.

results.title: Opponent moves stay in the winning region
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a parity game, let $v$ be a position in the winning region of player $p$ that is owned by the opponent of $p$. Then every position $w$ with a move from $v$ to $w$ is in the winning region of $p$.

results.title: A winning strategy's move stays in the winning region
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a parity game, let $\sigma$ be a positional strategy of player $p$ that wins from a position $v$ owned by $p$. Then the successor $\sigma(v)$ chosen by $\sigma$ is in the winning region of $p$.

results.title: Controllable predecessor
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $X$ a set of positions. The controllable predecessor $\mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ of $X$ for $p$ is the set of positions $v$ such that either $v$ is owned by $p$ and some move from $v$ leads into $X$, or $v$ is not owned by $p$ and every move from $v$ leads into $X$.

results.title: Attractor operator
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The attractor operator of $T$ for $p$ is the monotone map on sets of positions sending $X$ to $T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$.

results.title: Attractor
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The attractor of $T$ for $p$ is the least fixed point of the attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ on sets of positions, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$.

results.title: Attractor stages
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions and $n$ a natural number. The $n$-th attractor stage $S_n$ of $T$ for $p$ is the set obtained by applying the attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ $n$ times to $\emptyset$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$; thus $S_0 = \emptyset$ and $S_{n+1} = T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(S_n)$.

results.title: The attractor is a fixed point
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions, and let $A$ be the attractor of $T$ for $p$. Then $T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(A) = A$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p(A)$ is the controllable predecessor of $A$ for $p$; that is, $A$ is a fixed point of the attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$.

results.title: The attractor lies in every closed set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. If a set $X$ of positions satisfies $T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X) \subseteq X$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$, then the attractor of $T$ for $p$ is contained in $X$.

results.title: The attractor stabilizes after as many stages as there are positions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game with finitely many positions, $N$ of them, let $p$ be a player and $T$ a set of positions. Then the attractor of $T$ for $p$ equals the $N$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$, that is, the result of applying the attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ $N$ times to $\emptyset$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$.

results.title: Attractor strategy
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ is the positional strategy of $p$ that at a position $v$ moves to a successor of $v$ lying in the $n$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$, for the least $n$ for which $v$ has such a successor, and to an arbitrary successor of $v$ if no successor of $v$ lies in any attractor stage.

results.title: The attractor strategy moves into the stage from its controllable predecessor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions, $n$ a natural number and $S_n$ the $n$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$. If a position $v$ owned by $p$ lies in the controllable predecessor $\mathrm{cpre}_p(S_n)$ of $S_n$ for $p$, then the successor that the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ chooses at $v$ lies in $S_n$.

results.title: The attractor strategy reaches the target from an attractor stage
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions and $n$ a natural number. If $\pi$ is a play of $G$ that conforms to the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ and whose initial position $\pi_0$ lies in the $n$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$, then $\pi_i \in T$ for some $i < n$.

results.title: Forcing a visit to a set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $\sigma$ a positional strategy of $p$, $T$ a set of positions and $v$ a position. The strategy $\sigma$ forces a visit to $T$ from $v$ when every play $\pi$ of $G$ with $\pi_0 = v$ that conforms to $\sigma$ visits $T$, that is, $\pi_i \in T$ for some $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

results.title: The attractor strategy reaches the target from the attractor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game with finitely many positions, $N$ of them, let $p$ be a player and $T$ a set of positions. If $\pi$ is a play of $G$ that conforms to the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ and whose initial position $\pi_0$ lies in the attractor of $T$ for $p$, then $\pi_i \in T$ for some $i < N$.

results.title: The attractor strategy forces a visit
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game with finitely many positions, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. From every position $v$ of the attractor of $T$ for $p$, the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ forces a visit to $T$: every play from $v$ conforming to it visits $T$.

results.title: Trap for a player
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game and $p$ a player. A set $U$ of positions is a trap for $p$ when, for every position $v \in U$, every move from $v$ leads into $U$ if $v$ belongs to $p$, and some move from $v$ leads into $U$ if $v$ does not belong to $p$. Thus $p$ cannot force the play out of $U$.

results.title: The complement of an attractor is a trap
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The complement of the attractor of $T$ for $p$ is a trap for $p$.

results.title: Traps disjoint from a set avoid its attractor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. If a set $U$ of positions is a trap for $p$ and is disjoint from $T$, then $U$ is disjoint from the attractor of $T$ for $p$.

results.title: Trap strategy
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $U$ a set of positions. The trap strategy for $U$ is the positional strategy of the opponent of $p$ that, at each position $v$, moves to some position $w \in U$ with a move from $v$ to $w$ if there is one, and to an arbitrary position reachable from $v$ in one move otherwise.

results.title: The trap strategy stays in the trap
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $U$ a trap for $p$. If $\pi$ is a play with $\pi_0 \in U$ that conforms to the trap strategy of the opponent of $p$ for $U$, then $\pi_i \in U$ for every $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

results.title: The trap strategy avoids the target
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions and $A$ the attractor of $T$ for $p$. If $\pi$ is a play starting at a position outside $A$ that conforms to the trap strategy of the opponent of $p$ for the complement of $A$, then $\pi_i \notin T$ for every $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

results.title: No strategy forces a visit from outside the attractor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. If a position $v$ is not in the attractor of $T$ for $p$, then no positional strategy of $p$ forces a visit to $T$ from $v$.

results.title: Characterization of the attractor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game with finitely many positions, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. A position $v$ lies in the attractor of $T$ for $p$ if and only if some positional strategy of $p$ forces a visit to $T$ from $v$.

results.title: Winning regions are traps for the opponent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a parity game $G$, the winning region of a player $p$, the set of positions from which $p$ has a winning positional strategy, is a trap for the opponent of $p$.

results.title: Encoded parity game
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: An encoded finite parity game on the $n$ positions $0, \dots, n - 1$ consists of an owner for each position, given as a Boolean (false for the even player, true for the odd player), a move relation, given as a Boolean-valued $n \times n$ matrix, and a priority for each position, given as a natural number.

results.title: The parity game of a serial encoded game
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game on the positions $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which every position has a move to some position. The associated parity game has the same positions, moves and priorities, and a position is owned by the odd player if $G$ assigns it to the odd player and by the even player otherwise; every position has a move by the hypothesis on $G$.

results.title: Dual parity game
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The dual of an encoded parity game $G$ is the encoded parity game with the same positions and moves in which every position is owned by the other player than in $G$ and has priority one more than in $G$.

results.title: Controllable predecessor inside a set of positions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game, $p$ a player (encoded as a Boolean: false for even, true for odd), and $U$, $X$ sets of positions. The controllable predecessor of $X$ for $p$ inside $U$ is the set of positions $v \in U$ such that either $v$ is owned by $p$ and some move of $G$ goes from $v$ to a position of $U \cap X$, or $v$ is not owned by $p$ and every move of $G$ from $v$ to a position of $U$ ends in $X$.

results.title: Attractor inside a set of positions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game on $n$ positions, $p$ a player (encoded as a Boolean: false for even, true for odd), and $T$, $U$ sets of positions. The attractor of $T$ for $p$ inside $U$ is the set obtained from $\emptyset$ by applying $n$ times the map $X \mapsto (T \cap U) \cup \mathrm{CPre}_p^U(X)$, where $\mathrm{CPre}_p^U(X)$ is the controllable predecessor of $X$ for $p$ inside $U$.

results.title: Rank of a priority in a parity game
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The rank of a priority `p` among the distinct priorities occurring in the game: the number of distinct priorities `q < p` that occur.

results.title: Compressed priority
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game on the positions $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. The compressed priority of a natural number $p$ is $2r + (p \bmod 2)$, where $r$ is the rank of $p$ in $G$: the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur in $G$.

results.title: Priority compression
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ on $n$ positions, the compressed game has the same owners and moves as $G$ and gives each position $v$ the priority $2r + (q \bmod 2)$, where $q$ is the priority of $v$ in $G$ and $r$ is the number of distinct priorities occurring in $G$ that are smaller than $q$.

results.title: Priority ranks are below the number of priorities
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game, and for a natural number $p$ let the rank of $p$ be the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur in $G$. For every position $v$ of $G$, the rank of the priority of $v$ is strictly less than the number of distinct priorities that occur in $G$.

results.title: Strict monotonicity of priority ranks
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game, and for a natural number $p$ let the rank of $p$ be the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur in $G$. If $v$ and $w$ are positions of $G$ and the priority of $w$ is strictly less than the priority of $v$, then the rank of the priority of $w$ is strictly less than the rank of the priority of $v$.

results.title: Monotonicity of priority ranks
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game, and for a natural number $p$ let the rank of $p$ be the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur in $G$. If $v$ and $w$ are positions of $G$ and the priority of $w$ is at most the priority of $v$, then the rank of the priority of $w$ is at most the rank of the priority of $v$.

results.title: Bound on compressed priorities
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ on $n$ positions, every priority of the priority-compressed game of $G$ is strictly less than $2n$.

results.title: Priority compression preserves and reflects the order of priorities
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ and positions $v$, $w$, the priority of $v$ is smaller than the priority of $w$ in the priority-compressed game of $G$ if and only if it is smaller in $G$.

results.title: Priority compression preserves parity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ and every position $v$, the priority of $v$ in the priority-compressed game of $G$ has the same parity as the priority of $v$ in $G$.

results.title: Maximal priority on a set of positions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ and a set $U$ of positions, the maximal priority on $U$ is the largest priority of $G$ at a position of $U$, or $0$ if $U$ is empty.

results.title: Positions of maximal priority
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ and a set $U$ of positions, the positions of maximal priority in $U$ are the positions $v \in U$ whose priority equals the maximal priority of $G$ on $U$.

results.title: Computation DAG
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A computation DAG on $n$ unit-time tasks, numbered $0, \dots, n - 1$, assigns to each task $v$ a list of predecessors (the tasks $v$ waits for), each numbered below $v$; so the numbering is a topological order.

results.title: Depth of a task in a computation DAG
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The depth of a task $v$ is the number of tasks on a longest path ending at $v$: it is $1$ plus the largest depth of a predecessor of $v$, or $1$ if $v$ has no predecessors.

results.title: Span of a computation DAG
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The span of a computation DAG is the number of tasks on a longest path, that is, the largest depth of a task, and $0$ when there are no tasks.

results.title: Predecessors have smaller depth
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a computation DAG, if $u$ is a predecessor of $v$, then the depth of $u$ is strictly less than the depth of $v$.

results.title: Depths of an initial segment of tasks
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $k \le n$, the list of the depths of tasks $0, \dots, k - 1$ of a computation DAG on $n$ tasks, computed in topological order: the empty list for $k = 0$, and for $k + 1$ the list for $k$ followed by $1$ plus the largest entry of that list at a predecessor of task $k$ (or $1$ if task $k$ has no predecessors).

results.title: Table of depths
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The list of the depths of tasks $0, \dots, n - 1$ of a computation DAG on $n$ tasks, computed once each in topological order: the entry for task $k$ is $1$ plus the largest entry at a predecessor of $k$, or $1$ if $k$ has no predecessors.

results.title: The table of depths is correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every task $v$ of a computation DAG, the entry of the table of depths at position $v$ equals the depth of $v$.

results.title: Schedule of a computation DAG
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A schedule of a computation DAG on $n$ tasks on $p$ processors assigns to each task $v$ a step $t(v) \in \mathbb{N}$ in which it runs, such that $t(u) < t(v)$ whenever $u$ is a predecessor of $v$, and for every step $s$ at most $p$ tasks $v$ have $t(v) = s$.

results.title: Length of a schedule
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The length of a schedule is the number of steps it takes: one more than the latest step in which a task runs (steps are numbered from $0$), or $0$ if there are no tasks.

results.title: The work law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a computation DAG on $n$ tasks, every schedule of it on $p$ processors that takes $T$ steps satisfies $n \le p T$. In particular, for $p > 0$ the schedule takes at least $n / p$ steps.

results.title: Depth bounds the step of a task
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every schedule of a computation DAG on $p$ processors, with steps numbered from $0$, every task $v$ runs in a step $t$ with $\operatorname{depth}(v) \le t + 1$.

results.title: The span law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: No schedule is shorter than the span.

results.title: Level size
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a computation DAG and a natural number $d$, the size of level $d$ is the number of tasks of depth $d$.

results.title: Steps of a level
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a computation DAG and natural numbers $p$ and $d$, let $L_d$ be the number of tasks of depth $d$. The number of steps of level $d$ on $p$ processors is $\lceil L_d / p \rceil$ if $p \ge 1$, and $0$ if $p = 0$.

results.title: First step of a level
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a computation DAG and natural numbers $p$ and $d$, let $s_e$ be the number of steps of level $e$ on $p$ processors: $\lceil L_e / p \rceil$ if $p \ge 1$ and $0$ if $p = 0$, where $L_e$ is the number of tasks of depth $e$. The first step of level $d$ is $\sum_{e < d} s_e$.

results.title: Rank within a level
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a computation DAG, the rank of a task $v$ is the number of tasks of the same depth as $v$ with a smaller number than $v$. Taken in numbering order, the tasks of a level have ranks $0, 1, 2, \dots$

results.title: Step of a task in Brent's schedule
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG and $p$ a natural number. If $p \ge 1$, for each $d$ let $L_d$ be the number of tasks of depth $d$ and $o_d = \sum_{e < d} \lceil L_e / p \rceil$, and for each task $v$ let $r(v)$ be the number of tasks of the same depth as $v$ with a smaller number; the step of a task $v$ is $o_{\operatorname{depth}(v)} + \lfloor r(v) / p \rfloor$. If $p = 0$, the step of every task is $0$.

results.title: No step of Brent's level schedule mixes levels
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG and $p \ge 1$. If two tasks $u$ and $v$ run in the same step of Brent's level-by-level schedule on $p$ processors, then $u$ and $v$ have the same depth.

results.title: Ranks increase within a level
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a computation DAG, if tasks $u$ and $v$ have the same depth and $u$ has a smaller number than $v$, then the rank of $u$ is smaller than the rank of $v$, where the rank of a task is the number of tasks of the same depth with a smaller number. In particular, ranks are distinct within a level.

results.title: Brent's level schedule
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG and $p \ge 1$. For each $d$ let $L_d$ be the number of tasks of depth $d$ and $o_d = \sum_{e < d} \lceil L_e / p \rceil$, and for each task $v$ let $r(v)$ be the number of tasks of the same depth as $v$ with a smaller number. Brent's level schedule is the schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors that runs each task $v$ at step $o_{\operatorname{depth}(v)} + \lfloor r(v) / p \rfloor$.

results.title: Level $0$ is empty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In every computation DAG no task has depth $0$, so the number of tasks of depth $0$ is $0$.

results.title: Brent's theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG with $n$ tasks and span $D$, and let $p \ge 1$. If Brent's level schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors takes $T$ steps, then $pT \le n + (p - 1) D$, that is, $T \le (n - D)/p + D$.

results.title: Brent's theorem with the work and span laws
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG on $n$ unit-time tasks with span $D$, and let $p \ge 1$. Then some schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors has length $T$ with $pT \le n + (p - 1)D$, and every schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors has a length $T'$ with $n \le pT'$ (the work law) and $D \le T'$ (the span law).

results.title: Load of a step
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The load of step $t$ in a schedule $S$ of a computation DAG is the number of tasks that $S$ runs in step $t$.

results.title: Ready task
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a schedule $S$ of a task graph, a task $v$ is ready at step $t$ if $v$ runs in a step later than $t$ and every predecessor of $v$ runs in a step earlier than $t$.

results.title: Greedy schedule
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A schedule $S$ of a computation DAG on $p$ processors is greedy if, for every step $t$ and every task that is ready at step $t$, exactly $p$ tasks run in step $t$: a step leaves a ready task waiting only when all $p$ processors are busy.

results.title: Greediness need only be checked at the steps of the schedule
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $S$ be a schedule of a computation DAG on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. Then $S$ is greedy if and only if, for every step $t < T$ and every task $v$ that is ready at step $t$, exactly $p$ tasks run in step $t$.

results.title: Number of incomplete steps
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a schedule $S$ of a computation DAG on $p$ processors and a natural number $t$, the number of incomplete steps before step $t$ is the number of steps $s < t$ in which $S$ runs fewer than $p$ tasks.

results.title: Each incomplete step advances the critical path
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a greedy schedule, fewer than `depth v` incomplete steps precede the step of task `v`.

results.title: The step loads add up to the number of tasks
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a schedule $S$ of a task graph with $n$ tasks that takes $T$ steps, the numbers of tasks run in the steps $0, 1, \dots, T - 1$ add up to $n$.

results.title: Complete steps are bounded by the work
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG with $n$ tasks, and let $S$ be a schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. If $C$ is the number of steps $t < T$ in which $S$ runs at least $p$ tasks (the complete steps, where all $p$ processors are busy), then $pC \le n$.

results.title: A greedy schedule has at most $D$ incomplete steps
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG with span $D$, and let $S$ be a greedy schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. Then at most $D$ of the steps $t < T$ are incomplete, that is, run fewer than $p$ tasks.

results.title: Every step of a schedule has a task running at or after it
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $S$ be a schedule of a computation DAG on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps, numbered from $0$. For every step $t < T$ there is a task that $S$ runs at step $t$ or later.

results.title: A greedy schedule never idles
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $S$ be a greedy schedule of a task graph on $p$ processors that takes $T$ steps, numbered $0, \dots, T - 1$. Then every step $t < T$ of $S$ runs at least one task.

results.title: The greedy scheduling bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG with $n$ tasks and span $D$, and let $S$ be a greedy schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. Then $pT \le n + (p - 1)D$.

results.title: The work-span bound for greedy schedules
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a computation DAG with $n$ tasks and span $D$, and let $S$ be a greedy schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. Then $pT \le n + pD$, that is, $T \le n/p + D$ when $p \ge 1$.
